title: Validate the split and the feature outputs
prompt:
Before the features go to the model, the team wants proof that the split is clean and the feature tables agree with it.

Write `split_summary(ratings, users, movies)`. It returns one row of facts about the training and evaluation rows and the two feature tables, built with your earlier functions.
rules: `cutoff` is `CUTOFF`. `training_rows` and `evaluation_rows` count the rows of `training_interactions` and `evaluation_interactions`; `last_training_at` is the latest training `rated_at` and `first_evaluation_at` the earliest evaluation one (missing when there are none).
`featured_users` and `featured_movies` count the rows of `user_features` and `movie_features`; `cold_start_users` and `cold_start_movies` count their cold starts.
`cold_evaluation_rows` counts the evaluation rows whose member has no training row.
`features_match` is true when the `ratings` of `user_features` add up to `training_rows`, and so do those of `movie_features`.
`leak_free` is true when no `last_rated_at` in either feature table is on or after the cutoff.
Return one row with the columns of `SUMMARY_SCHEMA`.
hints: `training.agg(F.count("*"), F.max("rated_at")).first()` gives a count and a time as plain values in one job; do the same for the evaluation rows with `F.min`.
A `left_anti` join of the evaluation rows against the training members keeps the rows of members the model has never seen. Count rows, not members.

One `agg` per feature table can give its row count, its cold starts (sum `cold_start` cast to int), its total `ratings` and how many `last_rated_at` reach the cutoff. Put all twelve values in one tuple, in the schema's order.
explanation: Each fact checks one promise of the pipeline. `last_training_at` before the cutoff and `first_evaluation_at` on or after it show the split is by time. `features_match` shows the feature tables were built from exactly the training rows: if they came from all the ratings, their counts would add up to more. `leak_free` checks the same from the other side, through the latest time each feature has seen. `cold_evaluation_rows` tells the team how many test rows the model must answer with no history for that member, which is the cold-start problem in one number. Gathering each table's numbers in one `agg(...).first()` keeps the job to a handful of queries; caching the training rows, which four of them reuse, is the next saving if this ran on far more data.
